passages.text: GLACIERS, or ICE-VALLEYS, vast fields or masses of ice, formed in the valleys and on the sides of the high Alps, chiefly in Savoy and Switzerland.
They do not keep always the same bounds; in some years they advance into the valleys, overturning trees and covering the fields, and in others they retreat.
Some writers suppose that the whole mass of ice slides slowly down the slope upon its bed, being urged by its own weight, and loosened beneath by the water which flows from the heat of the earth.

Upon the surface of the ice are carried great quantities of stones and earth, fallen from the rocks above; and these, being left at the sides and lower end of the glacier, form long ridges, which the people of the country call moraines.

The great blocks of granite which are found scattered over the plains of the north of Germany, far from any mountain of the same stone, are thought to have been carried thither by the waters of the deluge, or by violent currents of the sea.
The glaciers are perpetual; for the summer heat melts only their surface, and the snows of each winter repair the loss.
A glacier is a persistent body of dense ice that is constantly moving downhill under its own weight. It forms where snow builds up over many years faster than it melts.
Glaciers move in two ways: the ice deforms and flows inside the glacier, and the whole glacier can slide over its bed, helped by meltwater at the base.
A glacier advances when more snow is added in its upper part than is lost by melting in its lower part, and it retreats when melting is greater than the supply.
Rock debris that falls onto a glacier or is torn from its bed is carried along and left in ridges called moraines at the sides and end of the ice.

Large boulders called glacial erratics were carried long distances by ice sheets during the ice ages and left far from the rock they came from. The erratics of northern Germany came from Scandinavia. In 1837 Louis Agassiz proposed that great sheets of ice had once covered much of northern Europe.
Most glaciers in the world have been retreating since the late 19th century, and the retreat has become faster in recent decades because of climate change.
Alpine glaciers grew during the Little Ice Age, a cool period that ended in the mid-19th century, and some advanced over farms and villages.
Glaciers and ice sheets together hold about 69 percent of the world's fresh water.

reasons: Rare terms appear in both: moraines, advance and retreat, slides on its bed, boulders far from their source.
Glacial erratic scores well but covers only the boulders.

alignments.label: Masses of ice

britannica.quote: vast fields or masses of ice, formed in the valleys and on the sides of the high Alps

wikipedia.quote: a persistent body of dense ice that is constantly moving downhill under its own weight

alignments.note: A change in language. The 1810 entry describes Alpine glaciers. Wikipedia defines a glacier anywhere by how it forms and moves.

alignments.label: Advance and retreat

britannica.quote: in some years they advance into the valleys

wikipedia.quote: A glacier advances when more snow is added in its upper part than is lost by melting

alignments.note: The observation holds. Wikipedia adds the cause: the balance of snowfall and melting.

alignments.label: Fields overrun by ice

britannica.quote: overturning trees and covering the fields

wikipedia.quote: some advanced over farms and villages

alignments.note: Both texts report damage to farm land. Inference: the 1810 writers saw the glaciers near their largest size of the Little Ice Age.

alignments.label: Sliding on the bed

britannica.quote: the whole mass of ice slides slowly down the slope upon its bed, being urged by its own weight

wikipedia.quote: the ice deforms and flows inside the glacier, and the whole glacier can slide over its bed

alignments.note: A change in knowledge. Sliding under its own weight is right, but the ice also flows inside the glacier. The 1810 entry does not know this second motion.

alignments.label: Water under the ice

britannica.quote: loosened beneath by the water which flows from the heat of the earth

wikipedia.quote: helped by meltwater at the base

alignments.note: Water at the base does help the ice slide. The 1810 entry gives only one source for that water.

alignments.label: Stones form moraines

britannica.quote: these, being left at the sides and lower end of the glacier, form long ridges, which the people of the country call moraines

wikipedia.quote: left in ridges called moraines at the sides and end of the ice

alignments.note: The same fact and the same word. Moraine came into science from the local Alpine name.

alignments.label: Boulders moved by water

britannica.quote: carried thither by the waters of the deluge, or by violent currents of the sea

wikipedia.quote: were carried long distances by ice sheets during the ice ages

alignments.note: A change in knowledge. Ice, not water, carried the granite blocks. The 1810 entry knew that glaciers carry stones but did not link the two.

alignments.label: Glaciers are perpetual

wikipedia.quote: Most glaciers in the world have been retreating since the late 19th century

alignments.note: Glaciers are not permanent. Many have shrunk a great deal since 1810, and some have gone.

alignments.label: Theory of ice ages

wikipedia.quote: In 1837 Louis Agassiz proposed that great sheets of ice had once covered much of northern Europe

alignments.note: New knowledge from after 1810. It explains the boulders that the 1810 entry gave to the sea.

suggestedQuestions: How did the 1810 entry explain the boulders on the plains of northern Germany?
Was the 1810 entry right that glaciers slide on their beds?
Are glaciers perpetual, as the 1810 entry said?

How did the 1810 entry explain the bould.answer: It said the deluge or strong sea currents carried them [B5]. Wikipedia says ice sheets carried these erratics from Scandinavia during the ice ages [W5]. Agassiz proposed the ice-age idea in 1837, after the 1810 entry [W5].

Was the 1810 entry right that glaciers s.answer: Partly. It said the ice slides down under its own weight, helped by water underneath [B3]. Wikipedia agrees that glaciers slide, helped by meltwater, but adds that the ice also deforms and flows inside the glacier [W2].

Are glaciers perpetual, as the 1810 entr.answer: No. The entry said winter snow repairs the summer loss [B6], though it also saw glaciers advance and retreat [B2]. Wikipedia says most glaciers have been retreating since the late 19th century, and faster in recent decades [W6].
